name: Adalaj Vav
description: Five-storeyed stepwell combining water storage, shaded access and Indo-Islamic/Hindu architectural traditions.
overview: Adalaj Vav is a subterranean water structure reached through multiple flights of steps. Its galleries and openings create shade and ventilation while providing access to water at different levels.

name: Rajon Ki Baoli
description: Historic Delhi stepwell restored as part of a major heritage water-system conservation initiative.
overview: Rajon Ki Baoli is a masonry stepwell in Mehrauli Archaeological Park. It demonstrates Delhi's historic use of stepped wells for water access and communal infrastructure; conservation work has included cleaning, desilting and structural repair.

name: Tanka
description: Underground household or community cistern designed to store collected rainwater for dry periods.
overview: Tankas are underground storage chambers that collect runoff from rooftops or prepared catchments. Their enclosed form protects stored water from evaporation and contamination, making them particularly suited to arid Rajasthan.

name: Khadin
description: Long earthen embankment system that captures runoff on agricultural land and supports soil-moisture storage.
overview: Khadin systems use low embankments across the lower slopes of arid catchments. Runoff is detained on agricultural fields, allowing moisture to infiltrate and support crop production after the rains.

name: Nadi
description: Community pond that stores seasonal runoff for livestock and local water needs.
overview: Nadis are village-scale ponds fed mainly by local runoff during the monsoon. They represent decentralized water storage adapted to arid and semi-arid settlement patterns.

name: Johad
description: Small earthen check dam that slows runoff and promotes groundwater recharge.
overview: Johads intercept monsoon runoff using earthen embankments. By slowing water movement, they encourage infiltration and help replenish shallow groundwater while creating seasonal surface storage.

name: Ahar-Pyne
description: Integrated reservoir and channel system used to capture monsoon runoff and distribute water to fields.
overview: An ahar is a storage basin while pynes are channels that convey water from rivers or drainage paths into agricultural areas. Together they form a landscape-scale system for floodwater capture and irrigation.

name: Eri System
description: Network of interconnected irrigation tanks that stores monsoon water and distributes it through a landscape.
overview: Eri tanks form linked storage systems in which surplus water can move from one tank to another. The network supports irrigation, groundwater recharge and flood moderation across village landscapes.

name: Oorani
description: Small village pond traditionally used for drinking water and local domestic needs.
overview: Ooranis are community water bodies, often designed to collect and retain rainwater. Their relatively localized scale made them important sources of domestic water in settlements.

name: Kere
description: Traditional village tank used for irrigation, livestock and groundwater recharge.
overview: Kere tanks store seasonal runoff and support agriculture and settlement water needs. In many landscapes, tanks form part of interconnected local drainage and irrigation systems.

name: Kalyani
description: Stepped temple water tank associated with ritual, community and water-storage functions.
overview: Kalyanis are stepped tanks commonly associated with temples. Their masonry edges provide controlled access while the tank can collect rainwater and serve ritual and community functions.

name: Surangam
description: Hand-dug horizontal tunnel that intercepts groundwater in lateritic hills and conveys it by gravity.
overview: Surangams are tunnel-like wells excavated into hill slopes. Groundwater enters through the tunnel walls and is collected or conveyed to storage without mechanical pumping.

name: Kuhl
description: Gravity-fed mountain channel carrying water from streams to agricultural terraces and settlements.
overview: Traditional kuhls divert water from mountain streams and guide it along carefully graded channels. Their operation depends on local terrain knowledge, community maintenance and gravity rather than pumping.

name: Naula
description: Masonry spring-water structure that protects and provides access to groundwater in Himalayan settlements.
overview: Naulas are small, often stone-built structures developed around natural springs. The enclosed or semi-enclosed form protects the spring and provides a stable point for collecting water.

name: Zing
description: Small storage reservoir that captures glacier meltwater for irrigation and domestic use.
overview: Zings are small tanks used to store seasonal meltwater in high-altitude settlements. They help regulate short-duration glacial flows and make water available for agriculture and household needs.

name: Zabo
description: Integrated land-and-water management system linking forested catchments, ponds, livestock areas and terraced fields.
overview: Zabo combines watershed protection, runoff collection, livestock management and agriculture. Water is guided through the landscape so that resources are reused across different stages before reaching fields.

name: Apatani Water Management
description: Integrated terrace agriculture and water-management system using controlled water movement across paddy fields.
overview: The Apatani system links forests, streams, terraces and agricultural plots through carefully managed water flows. It is notable for integrating irrigation with landscape and community resource management.

name: Cheruvu
description: Traditional tank or reservoir used to capture runoff and support irrigation and groundwater recharge.
overview: Cheruvus are village-scale reservoirs that capture seasonal runoff. They support irrigation and can recharge groundwater, forming part of traditional tank-based landscapes in the Deccan.

name: Bhandara
description: Small masonry or earthen diversion structure used to raise and divert river water toward fields.
overview: Bhandaras intercept flowing water and divert it into irrigation channels. They are adapted to seasonal river flows and traditionally relied on locally available construction methods.

name: Phad System
description: Community-managed irrigation system that diverts river water into distributary channels serving agricultural blocks.
overview: The Phad system organizes river diversion, channels, field distribution and community management as a coordinated irrigation network. Water allocation and maintenance are traditionally shared among users.

name: Ramtek Water Management
description: Historic network of tanks and catchments associated with Ramtek's settlement and temple landscape.
overview: Ramtek contains a long history of water structures integrated with the terrain and built environment. Tanks and associated catchments supported settlement, ritual activities and local water security.

name: Kallanai / Grand Anicut
description: Ancient masonry barrage across the Cauvery designed to divert river water into irrigation channels.
overview: Kallanai is an early large-scale river-diversion structure associated with Chola-period water engineering. Its primary role is to regulate and distribute Cauvery water to the delta irrigation network.

name: Bhojtal / Upper Lake
description: Large historic lake created to store water and support the settlement around Bhopal.
overview: Upper Lake is traditionally associated with King Bhoja and forms part of Bhopal's historic water landscape. Its large catchment and storage capacity have supported the city's water needs over centuries.

name: Chandela Tanks
description: Historic tank-building tradition using reservoirs to capture monsoon water in a semi-arid landscape.
overview: Chandela-era tanks were engineered to store monsoon runoff and support settlements and agriculture. Their masonry embankments and associated structures demonstrate landscape-scale water planning.

name: Virdas
description: Small wells excavated in sandy areas to collect fresh water that accumulates above saline groundwater.
overview: Virdas exploit local hydrogeology in arid Kutch. Fresh rainwater percolates through sand and can accumulate in a shallow freshwater lens, which is accessed through carefully dug wells.

name: Kund
description: Round or polygonal catchment and underground storage structure designed primarily for drinking-water collection.
overview: Kunds collect runoff from a prepared catchment and guide it into a covered underground chamber. Their geometry and protected storage reduce evaporation and contamination in arid environments.

name: Paar System
description: Landscape system in which rainwater percolates through sandy catchments and is later accessed through shallow wells.
overview: Paar systems use sandy terrain as a natural infiltration zone. Rainwater from an agar catchment percolates into the subsurface, where water can later be accessed through kuis or beris.

name: Khatri
description: Rock-cut or masonry cistern used to collect and store water in the Himalayan region.
overview: Khatris are traditional water-storage structures adapted to hill settlements and local geology. They provide protected storage where surface water availability varies seasonally.

name: Dongs
description: Traditional channels or small diversion arrangements used to convey water in Assam's riverine landscape.
overview: Dongs are locally adapted water-conveyance structures associated with the Brahmaputra valley. They illustrate how communities used simple channels to move water for agriculture and domestic needs.

name: Katas / Mundas / Bandhas
description: Traditional small reservoirs and embankments used to retain monsoon water for agriculture and local use.
overview: These structures use earth and locally available materials to retain seasonal runoff. Their distributed form allows villages to manage water close to where it falls.

name: Jackwell
description: Traditional well-based system adapted to high-rainfall island environments for collecting and storing freshwater.
overview: Jackwells are associated with traditional water collection in the islands and demonstrate adaptation to heavy rainfall, porous ground and freshwater availability constraints.
